chapter_sections.label: Definition:
chapter_sections.text: - STATISTICS is the branch of mathematics that deals with the collection, presentation, analysis, and interpretation of numerical data.

chapter_sections.label: Key Points:
points: Data can be represented in tables (already known) or graphically.
Graphical representation makes comparisons among individual items easier to understand than actual data.
"One picture is better than a thousand words" — graphical representation gives a better visual understanding.

chapter_sections.label: Definition:
chapter_sections.text: - A BAR GRAPH is a pictorial representation of data in which usually bars of uniform width are drawn with equal spacing between them on one axis (say, the x-axis), depicting the variable. The values of the variable are shown on the other axis (say, the y-axis) and the heights of the bars depend on the values of the variable.

chapter_sections.label: Key Points:
points: Bars are of uniform width.
Equal spacing (gaps) is maintained between consecutive bars.
x-axis: variable (categories/heads).
y-axis: value of the variable (frequency or quantity).
The width of the bar is not important — only the height matters.
Scale on y-axis is chosen based on maximum value to be represented.
From the heights of bars, relative comparisons can be made at a glance.
TRY THESE / FIGURE IT OUT:
Activity 1: Continuing with the same four groups of Activity 1, represent the data by suitable bar graphs.
A1: Students collect data in four groups from a previous activity. They represent the data on a bar graph:
x-axis: variable (categories from each group's data)
y-axis: value of each category
Bars of uniform width with equal spacing
Scale chosen based on maximum value
EXAMPLES: (textbook examples)
EXAMPLE 12.1.A.1: Bar Graph — Students born in different months
PROBLEM: In a particular section of Class IX, 40 students were asked about the months of their birth and the following bar graph (Fig. 12.1) was prepared. Observe the bar graph and answer:
(i) How many students were born in the month of November?
(ii) In which month were the maximum number of students born?
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Identify variable and value.
Variable = Month of birth. Value = Number of students born.
Step 2: Read the bar for November.
Height of November bar = 4 units.
Step 3: Find the tallest bar.
Tallest bar = August.
ANSWER:
(i) 4 students were born in the month of November.
(ii) The maximum number of students were born in the month of August.
EXAMPLE 12.1.A.2: Bar Graph — Family monthly expenditure
PROBLEM: A family with a monthly income of Rs. 20,000 had planned the following expenditures per month under various heads. Draw a bar graph for the data.
Table 12.1:
Heads                    | Expenditure (in thousand rupees)
Grocery                  | 4
Rent                     | 5
Education of children    | 5
Medicine                 | 2
Fuel                     | 2
Entertainment            | 1
Miscellaneous            | 1
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Represent Heads (variable) on horizontal axis. Take equal widths for all bars and equal gaps between them. Let 1 Head = 1 unit on x-axis.
Step 2: Represent expenditure (value) on vertical axis. Maximum expenditure = Rs. 5000. Choose scale: 1 unit = Rs. 1000.
Step 3: Draw rectangle for Grocery with width 1 unit and height 4 units (= Rs. 4000).
Step 4: Draw rectangles for remaining heads similarly, leaving gap of 1 unit between each.
ANSWER: Bar graph (Fig. 12.2) drawn with x-axis = Heads, y-axis = Expenditure (thousand rupees, scale 1 unit = Rs. 1000).
Observation: Expenditure on education is more than double that of medical expenses (5 vs 2 units).
ADDITIONAL CALCULATIONS:
Problem 1: From Table 12.1 (family expenditure), what fraction of total expenditure is spent on Rent?
Solution:
Total expenditure = 4 + 5 + 5 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 20 thousand rupees
Rent = 5 thousand rupees
Fraction = 5/20 = 1/4
Answer: 1/4 of total expenditure is spent on Rent.
Problem 2: In Example 1 (birth months), if 4 students were born in November and 6 in October, what would be the bar height for October if scale is 1 unit = 1 student?
Solution:
October frequency = 6 students.
Height of October bar = 6 units (since scale is 1 unit = 1 student).
Answer: October bar height = 6 units.

chapter_sections.label: Definition:
chapter_sections.text: - A HISTOGRAM is a graphical representation of a grouped frequency distribution with continuous classes. It is like a bar graph but used for continuous class intervals. In a histogram, rectangles are drawn with no gaps between them, where width = class size and area of each rectangle is proportional to the corresponding frequency.

chapter_sections.label: Key Points:
points: Unlike bar graphs, there are NO gaps between consecutive rectangles in a histogram.
The area of each rectangle is proportional to the corresponding frequency.
When class widths are equal: heights are proportional to frequencies (draw heights = frequencies directly).
When class widths are varying: heights must be adjusted so areas remain proportional to frequencies.
Adjusted height = (Frequency / Width of class) x Minimum class size
A kink or break on the axis is shown if the first class interval does not start from zero.
The y-axis label for varying-width histogram: "proportion of students per [minimum class size] interval."
Steps to draw histogram (uniform width):
(i) Represent variable on horizontal axis. If first class does not start from 0, show kink.
(ii) Represent frequency on vertical axis on suitable scale.
(iii) Draw rectangles of width = class-size and height = frequency.
(iv) No gaps between consecutive rectangles.
Steps to draw histogram (varying width):
Step 1: Select class interval with minimum class size.
Step 2: Adjusted height = (Frequency / Width of class) x Minimum class size.

chapter_sections.label: FORMULA:
items: Adjusted height (varying width histogram) = (Frequency / Width of class) x Minimum class size
Frequency = number of observations in that class
Width of class = upper limit - lower limit of that class interval
Minimum class size = smallest class width among all class intervals
EXAMPLE 12.1.B.1: Histogram — Uniform width (weights of 36 students)
PROBLEM: Draw a histogram for the following frequency distribution representing the weights of 36 students:
Step 1: Represent weights on horizontal axis. Scale: 1 cm = 5 kg. Since first class starts from 30.5 (not 0), show a kink (break) on the axis.
Step 2: Represent number of students (frequency) on vertical axis. Maximum = 15.
Step 3: Draw rectangles — all class widths = 5 kg (equal width). Heights = frequencies directly.
Step 4: No gaps between consecutive rectangles → histogram (Fig. 12.3).
ANSWER: Histogram drawn. Class 40.5-45.5 has the tallest bar (frequency = 15).
EXAMPLE 12.1.B.2: Histogram — Varying width (marks of 90 students)
PROBLEM: A teacher grouped students' marks (out of 100) into varying class intervals. Show the histogram using heights directly is WRONG and draw the correct histogram.
Step 1: Class widths vary (0-20 has width 20; 70-100 has width 30; others width 10). Using heights = frequencies directly gives misleading Fig. 12.4.
Step 2: Minimum class size = 10. Calculate adjusted heights:
Step 3: Draw correct histogram (Fig. 12.5) with adjusted heights. y-axis: "Proportion of students per 10 marks interval."
ANSWER: Correct histogram drawn. Adjusted heights: 3.5, 10, 10, 20, 20, 15, 2.67.
Problem 1: In Table 12.2, what is the total number of students with weight less than 40.5 kg?
Answer: 15 students have weight less than 40.5 kg.
Problem 2: Verify adjusted height for 40-50 (freq=20, width=10, min class size=10).

chapter_sections.label: Definition:
chapter_sections.text:
- A FREQUENCY POLYGON is a graphical representation of quantitative data using a polygon (closed figure) formed by joining the mid-points (class-marks) of the tops of the rectangles in a histogram by line segments. It can also be drawn without a histogram using class-marks directly.
- CLASS-MARK is the mid-point of a class interval.
Formula: CLASS-MARK = (Upper limit + Lower limit) / 2

chapter_sections.label: Key Points:
points: Frequency polygons can be drawn in two ways:
Method 1 (With histogram): Join mid-points (class-marks) of tops of adjacent histogram rectangles.
Method 2 (Without histogram): Plot (class-mark, frequency) points directly and join them.
To complete the polygon, add imaginary class intervals with zero frequency:
Before the first class and after the last class.
Adding zero-frequency classes at both ends makes area of frequency polygon equal to area of histogram.
If first class is 0-10, imaginary preceding class is (-10)-0 with class-mark = -5.
Frequency polygons are used when data is continuous and very large.
Very useful for comparing two different sets of data of the same nature.

chapter_sections.label: FORMULA:
items: Upper limit = upper boundary of the class interval
Lower limit = lower boundary of the class interval
EXAMPLE 12.1.C.1: Frequency Polygon — From histogram (marks of 51 students)
PROBLEM: Draw a frequency polygon for marks of 51 students (Table 12.5).
Step 1: Draw histogram. Mark mid-points of tops as B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K.
Step 2: Imaginary preceding class = (-10)-0. Class-mark = -5. Frequency = 0. Join B to (-5, 0); where line meets y-axis = point A.
Step 3: Imaginary succeeding class = 100-110. Class-mark = 105. Frequency = 0. Mark as L.
Step 4: Join O, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L → frequency polygon OABCDEFGHIJKL (Fig. 12.7).
ANSWER: Class 10-20 has highest frequency (10). Total = 51 students. ✓
EXAMPLE 12.1.C.2: Frequency Polygon — Without histogram (cost of living index)
PROBLEM: Draw frequency polygon for cost of living index data (Table 12.6) WITHOUT histogram.
Step 1: Find class-marks (shown in Table 12.7 above).
Step 5: Join all → frequency polygon ABCDEFGH (Fig. 12.8).
ANSWER: Class 160-170 has highest frequency (20 weeks). Total = 52 weeks. ✓
Problem 1: Find class-mark of 600-700 (from Exercise 12.1 Q5).
Problem 2: In Example 12.1.C.2, verify total weeks = 52.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text: - GRAPHICAL REPRESENTATION is a method of presenting data in the form of pictures or graphs. It makes comparisons among individual items easier to understand than actual data or tables.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Data represented by tables has already been studied in earlier classes.
Graphical representation gives a better visual understanding — "one picture is better than a thousand words."
Comparisons among individual items are best shown by means of graphs.
Three types of graphical representations are studied in this topic:
(A) Bar graphs
(B) Histograms of uniform width, and of varying widths
(C) Frequency polygons

sections.label: LIST OF SUB TOPICS IN THIS TOPIC:

items.question: Define graphical representation of data. Why is it better than tabular form?
items.answer:
GRAPHICAL REPRESENTATION is a method of presenting data in the form of pictures or graphs. It makes comparisons among individual items easier to understand than actual data or tables.
It is better than tabular form because: one can easily visualise relative characteristics of data at a glance. As the textbook states — "one picture is better than a thousand words."

items.question: Name the three types of graphical representations studied in Topic 12.1.
items.answer:
The three types of graphical representations studied are:
(A) Bar graphs — for discrete / categorical data.
(B) Histograms of uniform width, and of varying widths — for continuous grouped data.
(C) Frequency polygons — for continuous large data, especially to compare two data sets.

items.question: What is the importance of the width of a bar in a bar graph versus a histogram?
items.answer:
In a Bar Graph:
The width of the bar is NOT important. Only the height (value) matters. All bars have uniform width just for visual clarity.

In a Histogram:
The width of the bar IS significant — it equals the class-size. The area of each rectangle (width x height) is proportional to the corresponding frequency. Different class widths require adjusted heights.

items.question: For what purpose are frequency polygons most suitable?
items.answer:
Frequency polygons are most suitable:
1. When data is continuous and very large.
2. When comparing two different sets of data of the same nature, for example, comparing the performance of two different sections of the same class on the same graph.

---

3 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 2 questions:

items.question: Explain the two methods of drawing a frequency polygon. Which method is used when the class intervals start from 0-10?
items.answer:
Step 1: Method 1 — With Histogram.
Draw the histogram first. Mark the mid-points (class-marks) of the tops of each rectangle. Join these mid-points by line segments. Add imaginary zero-frequency class at both ends to close the polygon.

Step 2: Method 2 — Without Histogram.
Find class-marks (= (Upper + Lower)/2) for each class interval. Plot the points (class-mark, frequency) directly. Add imaginary zero-frequency classes at both ends. Join all points by line segments.

Step 3: When first class = 0-10.
Imaginary preceding class = (-10)-0. Class-mark = (-10+0)/2 = -5. Frequency = 0.
Join point B (class-mark 5, first frequency) to this point. Where this line meets the y-axis is marked as A. Polygon begins from A on the y-axis.

items.question: In a bar graph of a family's monthly expenditure, Grocery = Rs.4000, Rent = Rs.5000, Education = Rs.5000, Medicine = Rs.2000, Fuel = Rs.2000, Entertainment = Rs.1000, Miscellaneous = Rs.1000. (i) What scale is chosen for y-axis? (ii) Which head has maximum expenditure? (iii) How does the graph help compare items?
items.answer:
Step 1: Choose scale for y-axis.
Maximum expenditure = Rs.5000. Choose scale: 1 unit = Rs.1000. y-axis goes up to 5 units.

Step 2: Head with maximum expenditure.
Both Rent and Education of children are highest at Rs.5000 each (height = 5 units).

Step 3: Comparison using graph.
From bar heights directly: Education (5 units) is more than double that of Medicine (2 units). Fuel equals Medicine (both 2 units). Entertainment equals Miscellaneous (both 1 unit). This comparison is immediate from the graph but would take more effort in a table.

4 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 3 questions:

items.question: The following data shows the marks obtained by 40 students in a test. The class intervals are given but are NOT continuous. (i) Make them continuous. (ii) Draw a histogram. (iii) State which class has maximum frequency. (iv) Can we say the maximum marks scored are 153 mm? Justify.
items.answer:
Step 1: Make class intervals continuous.
Subtract 0.5 from lower limit; add 0.5 to upper limit.

Original  | Continuous      | Freq
118-126   | 117.5-126.5    | 3
127-135   | 126.5-135.5    | 5
136-144   | 135.5-144.5    | 9
145-153   | 144.5-153.5    | 12
154-162   | 153.5-162.5    | 5
163-171   | 162.5-171.5    | 4
172-180   | 171.5-180.5    | 2

All class widths = 9 (equal). Heights = frequencies directly.

Step 2: Draw histogram.
x-axis: Length (mm); y-axis: Number of leaves.
Show kink at start since data begins at 117.5, not 0.
Rectangles: heights 3, 5, 9, 12, 5, 4, 2; width = 9 for each. No gaps.

Step 3: Class with maximum frequency.
Class 144.5-153.5 (original 145-153) has the highest frequency = 12 leaves.

Step 4: Can we say maximum leaves are 153 mm?
NO. The class 144.5-153.5 has the maximum frequency of 12, but these 12 leaves can have any length between 144.5 mm and 153.5 mm — they are not all exactly 153 mm long. So the statement is incorrect.

items.question: In a particular section of Class IX, 40 students were asked about their birth months. The bar graph (Fig. 12.1) shows: August = 6 students (maximum), November = 4 students.
items.answer:
Step 1: Total monthly expenditure.
= 4 + 5 + 5 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 20 thousand rupees = Rs.20,000.

Step 2: Steps to draw bar graph.
(i) Draw x-axis: Heads (Grocery, Rent, Education, Medicine, Fuel, Entertainment, Miscellaneous). Let 1 unit = 1 head.
(ii) Draw y-axis: Expenditure. Scale: 1 unit = Rs.1000. Maximum = Rs.5000 → y-axis up to 5 units.
(iii) Draw rectangle for Grocery: width = 1 unit, height = 4 units.
(iv) Draw remaining bars with gap of 1 unit between each.

Step 3: Item equal to Rent.
Rent = Rs.5000. Education of children = Rs.5000.
Education of children equals Rent in expenditure.

Step 4: More spent on Education than Medicine.
Education = Rs.5000, Medicine = Rs.2000.
Difference = 5000 - 2000 = Rs.3000.
Education costs Rs.3000 more per month than Medicine.
Also: Education is 5000/2000 = 2.5 times the medicine expenditure.

items.question: The runs scored by two cricket teams A and B on the first 60 balls are given below. The class intervals are given as discrete. (i) Make them continuous. (ii) Write the class-marks. (iii) Write the coordinates (class-mark, frequency) for Team A's frequency polygon including imaginary end points.

PART A — Bar Graph: Causes of Illness Among Women:

Step 1: Draw bar graph.
x-axis: Causes (S.No. 1 to 6), y-axis: Female fatality rate (%).
Scale: 1 unit = 5% (maximum = 31.8%, so y-axis up to approximately 7 units = 35%).
Bars: 31.8, 25.4, 12.4, 4.3, 4.1, 22.0.

Step 2: Major cause.
Reproductive health conditions has the highest bar (31.8%) → it is the major cause of illness and death among women worldwide.

Step 3: Total of all percentages.
31.8 + 25.4 + 12.4 + 4.3 + 4.1 + 22.0 = 100%.
This confirms that the data accounts for ALL causes of women's illness and death — the percentages add up to 100%, which is expected for a complete survey.

PART B — Histogram: Surnames and Number of Letters:

Step 1: Note class widths are varying.
1-4 → width = 3
4-6 → width = 2
6-8 → width = 2
8-12 → width = 4
12-20 → width = 8
Minimum class size = 2.

Step 2: Calculate adjusted heights.
Adjusted height = (Frequency / Width) x Minimum class size = (Frequency / Width) x 2.

Letters | Freq | Width | Calculation         | Adj. Height
1-4     |  6   |   3   | (6/3) x 2 = 4       | 4
4-6     | 30   |   2   | (30/2) x 2 = 30     | 30
6-8     | 44   |   2   | (44/2) x 2 = 44     | 44
8-12    | 16   |   4   | (16/4) x 2 = 8      | 8
12-20   |  4   |   8   | (4/8) x 2 = 1       | 1

Step 3: Class with maximum adjusted height.
Class 6-8 has the maximum adjusted height = 44.

Step 4: Class with maximum number of surnames.
Class 6-8 has the maximum number of surnames = 44. (In this case, adjusted height and frequency are the same since width = minimum class size = 2.)

Answer:
(i) Adjusted heights: 4, 30, 44, 8, 1.
(ii) Class 6-8 has maximum adjusted height (44).
(iii) Class 6-8 has maximum number of surnames (44 surnames).
